got_through:
I built the whole Stage 1 specification from the paper and it is mostly there. Writing it out as I would hand it to my own code:

STATE SPACE AND RATE MATRIX. Two states, closed C and open O, ordered (C,O). k_on = 10 uM^-1 s^-1 multiplying [A], k_off = 100 s^-1 agonist independent. So Q(0 uM) = [[0,0],[100,-100]] s^-1 and Q(10 uM) = [[-100,100],[100,-100]] s^-1, P(t) = exp(Qt). This checks against two independent statements in the paper: the relaxation at agonist is k_on[A]+k_off = 200 s^-1, and P_open = 0.5 at agonist. Both come out right, so the rate matrix is pinned.

CONDUCTANCE TO CURRENT. Only O conducts, gamma = (0, i) with i = g = 1, baseline b = 1, both in units of g, g ~ 1 pA. Predicted mean per interval is N_ch * (interval-mean occupancy dotted into the interval-mean conductance) + b.

PROTOCOL. Single concentration jump, three segments 0 / 10 / 0 uM, 20:40:40 percent of the steps, total record 100 ms fixed across the whole interval sweep, raw sampling f_s = 50 kHz throughout. So 20 ms pre-pulse, 40 ms agonist, 40 ms washout. All channels closed at t=0, occupancy (1,0). Since [A]=0 in the pre-pulse and k_on[A] vanishes identically there, the pre-pulse contains no gating at all, which the paper confirms independently by reporting the noise level as informative at 20 pre-agonist intervals against 0 for k_on and i.

OBSERVABLE. ybar_t = b + (1/Delta) * integral over the window of the summed population conductance + eta_t, uniform (boxcar) weighting, no analogue filter simulated.

NOISE. Gaussian, white, per recorded value, variance e_t = Current_Noise / Delta_t = Current_Noise * f_s / n_samp. Current_Noise is the engine parameter in g^2 s; label = 1000 * Current_Noise exactly; dimensionless S_tilde = Current_Noise * k_off / i^2 = label/10. Reference cell label 0.1 gives Current_Noise = 1e-4 g^2 s and S_tilde = 0.01. Pink and proportional noise are zero.

SAMPLING. Delta*k_off in {1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01} realised as {500, 250, 100, 50, 25, 10, 5} raw samples per recorded value, i.e. Delta in {10, 5, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1} ms, giving {10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000} recorded samples in the 100 ms record. Every one of these is arithmetically consistent with f_s = 50 kHz and with tau = 1/k_off = 10 ms, and 20:40:40 divides all seven step counts into integers.

SIMULATOR. Uniformization of the two-state generator, per channel, with Lambda = max_i |q_ii| = 100 s^-1 in both segments: draw N ~ Poisson(Lambda T) per segment, place event times uniformly, jump on the embedded chain I + Q/Lambda, keep the resulting sojourns and integrate the piecewise-constant conductance exactly over each acquisition window. Ensembles: 10^4 recordings per maximum-likelihood grid cell (least squares included), 1000 for the time-resolved run.

WHAT ONE RECORDING LOOKS LIKE, at the paper's reference cell (N_ch = 100, label 0.1, Delta*k_off = 0.1): 100 ms, 100 recorded samples of 1 ms each, values in units of g (about 1 pA). Samples 1 to 20 are baseline 1 with s.d. sqrt(1e-4/1e-3) = 0.316. Samples 21 to 60 rise with time constant 5 ms to a plateau of amplitude N*p*i = 50 with per-sample s.d. sqrt(0.1 + 100*0.25*0.9366) = 4.85, where 0.9366 is the boxcar reduction factor 2(lambda*Delta - 1 + exp(-lambda*Delta))/(lambda*Delta)^2 at lambda*Delta = 0.2. Samples 61 to 100 decay with time constant 10 ms. At N_ch = 10^4 the same cell gives amplitude 5000 with per-sample s.d. about 48.

CHECKS I WOULD RUN. (a) Ensemble mean against the analytic two-state ODE, p_O(t) = 0.5(1 - exp(-200t)) rising and p_O(0)exp(-100t) decaying. Self-check, no paper number. (b) Ensemble variance of a recorded interval against the paper's own van Loan construction: Var(ybar_t) = N_ch * [ mu_0' (2 F_2(Delta) 1)/Delta^2 - (mu_0' F_1(Delta) 1 / Delta)^2 ] + e_t, with F_1 and F_2 read out of the (1,2) and (1,3) blocks of exp(Q_2 Delta) and exp(Q_3 Delta). The paper does give me these, in Eqs. augmented and gammabar-vbar, including the 0/0 endpoint-average limit I need in the pre-pulse. Self-check, no paper number. (c) The nearest thing to a printed reference, which is a joint simulator-plus-least-squares number and which does work: with a plug-in constant variance sigma^2 = SSE/n, the least-squares total log-likelihood is -(n/2)(1 + log 2 pi sigma^2), so the paper's -262 at n = 100 implies sigma^2 = 11.04; my record-average variance from the model above is 12.4 at the truth and about 11.7 once six free parameters take their share, which is 6 percent. Two more of the paper's numbers fall out of the same arithmetic: IR's quoted standard error +/-0.24 over 1000 recordings means s.d. 7.6 across recordings against sqrt(n/2) = 7.07 for a correctly calibrated 100-interval Gaussian, and the least-squares +/-0.73 means s.d. 23, which needs an effective d.o.f. of about 7 in the SSE, which is what the paper's own integrated residual autocorrelation of 9.26 gives (67/9.26 = 7.2). Three printed numbers that are mutually consistent with the model I built, which is a genuine verification route.
stopped_at: Two places. First, at building the sweep: I have the seven acquisition intervals and the eleven channel counts explicitly, but the paper never lists the instrumental-noise levels and contradicts itself on how many there are, so I cannot instantiate the grid the results are computed over. Second, at verifying the simulator on its own: there is no printed statistic of the simulated recordings alone anywhere in the nine files, so I can only check my simulator by implementing least squares first and matching a joint quantity, which does not separate a simulator bug from a likelihood bug. I carried on past both and the model, protocol, noise, sampling and simulator are otherwise fully specified and internally consistent.

blockers.object_or_step: The instrumental-noise axis of the sweep: the list of noise labels, and the cell set
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "Across the three directories, \texttt{IR} covers $N_{\mathrm{ch}} \in \{5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000\}$ and noise labels from $0.05$ to $10^6$". Results: "the boundary-conditioned member spans eleven channel counts from $5$ to $10^4$ across eleven noise levels, not on a full rectangle, and the others cover less." Discussion: "spanning eleven channel counts from $5$ to $10^4$ and twelve instrumental noise levels with seven acquisition intervals resolved inside each cell". And: "The figure code auto-detects which cells exist on disk at render time and prints the detected grid into the render log, so the cell set behind each figure is recoverable from that log."
blockers.what_you_still_need: The explicit list of noise labels, and the explicit (N_ch, label, Delta) cell set. The channel-count list is given as a set and the interval list as a set; the noise list is given only as a range, and the two counts of it disagree (eleven in Results, twelve in Discussion). The cell count that is quoted, 560 for IR, is neither 11*11*7 = 847 nor 11*12*7 = 924, and the paper says the grid is deliberately not rectangular, so I cannot back it out. The render log the paper points me at is not one of the nine files.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: {0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1, 10, 1e2, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5, 1e6}, eleven labels, with the top labels run only at the larger channel counts. The weak point of the guess is the jump from 1 straight to 10 with no 2 and no 5, which breaks the 1-2-5 pattern the low end follows. If the guess is wrong, every median-over-the-noise-sweep in Results moves, every fitted log-log crossing in Figure 6 moves (each is fitted through only four measured crossings), and the denominators 2268, 980, 896 and 336 cannot be reproduced at all.

blockers.object_or_step: Verifying the simulator on its own, against any number the paper prints
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "This is what licenses treating the simulation as the reference against which the Gaussian likelihood approximations are judged: the approximations are the object under test, and the simulator supplies the exact answer they are compared to." And: "The simulation seed was set to $0$, which in this engine is the sentinel for a random seed drawn from \texttt{std::random\_device}, and the resolved seed was never logged. The deposited ensembles are therefore statistically equivalent to, but not bit-for-bit reproducible from, a rerun of the same script." No sentence anywhere gives a statistic of the simulated data alone: no mean or peak current at a stated time, no variance of a recorded interval at a named cell, no open probability, no autocorrelation of the recorded current.
blockers.what_you_still_need: One printed number that is a property of the recordings and of nothing else, at a named cell. Every printed quantity that touches the data (the -262 / -230 / -147 / -143 log-likelihoods, the 0.9995 and 0.782 mean squared standardized residuals, the 1.008 / 1.30 / 3.93 / 9.26 integrated residual autocorrelations, the +0.183889 per-step ratio) requires at least one likelihood member to be implemented as well, so a simulator error and a likelihood error land on the same number and cannot be told apart. The paper also removes the trace-by-trace route by disclosing that the seed is random.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: I would proceed by self-checking against the analytic mean (the two-state ODE) and the analytic interval-average variance (the paper's own van Loan blocks), then implement least squares and hit -262 as a joint check, which I did on paper and which comes out to 6 percent. That is enough to convince me, but it is a check I only get after a whole extra implementation, and if it failed I would not know which half was wrong. What the paper should print is the variance of a recorded interval at the reference cell, one number, which would isolate the simulator completely and would also settle two of the ambiguities below.

blockers.object_or_step: The integrated autocorrelation of the standardized residual, the one quoted statistic that is nearly a property of the simulated data alone
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Results: "The integrated autocorrelation of the standardized residual, which counts how many intervals a likelihood effectively has for every interval it believes it has, reads $1.008$ for \texttt{IR}, $1.30$ for \texttt{R}, $3.93$ for \texttt{NR} and $9.26$ for \texttt{LSE} at noise label $0.1$." Diagnostics defines a related object: "the ratio $\kappa=\mathrm{Var}(L)\big/\sum_t\mathrm{Var}(X_t)$ is unity when the terms are independent". Methods: "The diagnostic battery used $100$ bootstrap replicates and a maximum lag of $10$ for the score autocorrelation".
blockers.what_you_still_need: Which channel counts and which acquisition intervals the quoted value is aggregated over, and by what estimator. The sentence names only the noise label. For least squares the standardized residual is the raw recorded current about the deterministic mean divided by one constant, so its integrated autocorrelation is essentially a simulator property, which makes this my only near-direct check; but it is quoted as a single number for a quantity that varies by almost an order of magnitude across the seven acquisition intervals. The max-lag of 10 is stated for the score autocorrelation, not for the residual one.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: kappa = Var(sum of r_t) / sum of Var(r_t) truncated at lag 10, median over the four channel counts and quoted at one acquisition interval rather than medianed over all seven. Reasoning: at Delta*k_off = 0.1 the lag-one residual correlation is exp(-lambda*Delta) = 0.82 and the truncated sum gives 8.86, close to 9.26; medianed over all seven intervals it would be far smaller, since at Delta*k_off = 1 the same formula gives 1.31. If the guess is wrong I lose my one direct simulator check and I cannot tell whether a mismatch is my trajectory generator or my binning.

blockers.object_or_step: The substep sampler used for Figure 1
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "the single-recording illustration (Figure~1) was drawn by the substep sampler instead, one $20$-channel trace at $250$ substeps per interval, and does not enter the quantitative comparison." Also: "The production scripts do pass a \texttt{number\_of\_substeps} argument, and on this branch it has no effect: the simulation parameters are built from the algorithm name alone, and the substep count they carry is zero."
blockers.what_you_still_need: The algorithm. "250 substeps per interval" names a discretisation and nothing else: whether each substep is a draw from the exact discrete-time transition matrix P(Delta/250) applied to each channel, or an Euler/tau-leap step, or something that also affects how the conductance is integrated within the substep. The paper explicitly contrasts it with the uniformization path ("Uniformization draws the transition times themselves, so there is no within-interval discretisation to choose and none to justify") but never says what the alternative does.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Exact discrete-time propagation of each channel's state by P(Delta/250), with the conductance held constant across each substep, so the interval average is a 250-point Riemann sum. If the guess is wrong Figure 1 does not reproduce, but the paper is explicit that Figure 1 carries no quantitative claim, so nothing measured moves.

blockers.object_or_step: Figure 1's recording: its length, its jump time, its acquisition interval and its noise level
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Figure 1 caption: "Two measurement windows are shown (6 to 10 ms of a 12 ms recording)." Its supplement: "The same filter cycle over the first ten milliseconds of the recording, so that the concentration jump and the onset of gating are inside the window." Against Methods: "The total record duration is held fixed at $100\;\mathrm{ms}$ across the sweep, so the interval is varied without varying the amount of data. Within each record the pre-pulse, agonist and post-pulse segments hold a fixed ratio of $20{:}40{:}40$ percent of the steps."
blockers.what_you_still_need: Figure 1's own protocol. Methods states one protocol, 100 ms with 20:40:40, and Figure 1 is on a 12 ms record with the jump inside the first ten milliseconds, so the Methods protocol does not describe it. The jump time, the acquisition interval and the noise label for that trace are given in no sentence.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Delta = 2 ms (two windows spanning 6 to 10 ms), Delta*k_off = 0.2, 12 ms record with 20:40:40 giving a jump at 2.4 ms, noise label 0.1 to match the reference cell used everywhere else. Wrong guesses give a figure that looks different and change nothing quantitative, but Figure 1 is the paper's only picture of what a recording looks like, so it is also the only thing I could eyeball my simulator against.

blockers.object_or_step: Whether N_ch is an exact channel count per recording or the mean of a distribution
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods calls it a mean: "while the white-noise level and the mean channel number were swept (below)", and lists among the six free parameters "the current baseline and the mean channel number". Theory and Results call it a count: "We write $N_{\mathrm{ch}}$ for the number of channels" and "$N_{\mathrm{ch}}$ is the number of channels in the patch". No sentence says whether the simulator draws it.
blockers.what_you_still_need: A statement that each recording contains exactly N_ch channels, or the distribution it is drawn from. The parameter is named "mean channel number" throughout Methods and there is no second parameter for its dispersion among the six, so if it is random the distribution is fixed-form and unnamed.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Deterministic, exactly N_ch channels in every recording. The reason is that the predictive variance in Eq. pred-var has three terms and none of them is proportional to the square of the mean current, which is what channel-number dispersion would contribute. If the guess is wrong the damage is concentrated exactly where the paper's headline result lives: with N Poisson at p = 0.5 the variance becomes N*i^2*p = 0.5*N instead of the gating-only N*p(1-p) = 0.25*N, a factor of two in the predictive variance at N_ch = 5, 10 and 20, which is the few-channel corner where region 0 and the departure of the boundary-conditioned member are measured.

blockers.object_or_step: The sign flip on the single-channel current
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "Only the open state conducts, and the code applies a sign flip so the single-channel current is inward." And, two paragraphs later: "the predicted current has mean $\bar y_t = N_{\mathrm{ch}}\,\mu_t\!\cdot\!\gamma_t + b$". No equation says where the flip is applied.
blockers.what_you_still_need: Whether gamma = (0, -i) with the baseline added afterwards, or the flip is applied to the whole N_ch*mu*gamma term, or to the recorded value including the baseline. With b = +1 and a negative unitary current the trace runs from +1 down to 1 - N_ch/2; with the flip applied last it runs the other way.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: gamma = (0, -i) and y = b + N_ch * (interval-mean conductance), so the baseline is not flipped. Nothing measured moves if this is wrong: the distortion matrix C = H^{-1/2} J H^{-1/2} is invariant under a diagonal sign change of the parameters, since H and J both transform as D H D, so all eigenvalues and all diagonal entries are unchanged. What is wrong is only the picture: my trace is upside down relative to the paper's.

blockers.object_or_step: Whether a recorded value is the exact time integral over the window or a block mean of raw samples on the 50 kHz grid
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Two Methods sentences pull opposite ways. "Each recorded measurement is the mean of $n_{\mathrm{samp},t}$ consecutive raw samples, so the averaging window is fixed at acquisition." And: "Uniformization draws the transition times themselves, so there is no within-interval discretisation to choose and none to justify." Theory writes the observable as an integral: "$\bar{y}_t = \frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{t-\Delta}^{t} y(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau + \eta_t$".
blockers.what_you_still_need: One sentence naming which object the simulator forms. This matters in principle because the whole interval-signal closure and the telegraphic regime are claims about this object.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: The exact integral of the piecewise-constant conductance over the window, on the strength of the uniformization sentence. I checked whether the choice bites and it does not: at the fastest rate in the study (lambda = k_on[A] + k_off = 200 s^-1) and the raw spacing of 20 us, the variance of the single-channel interval-mean conductance at the shortest window (Delta = 0.1 ms, 5 raw samples) is 0.24834 for the exact integral against 0.24840 for the 5-point mean, a difference of 0.02 percent, because lambda times the raw spacing is 0.004 everywhere in the sweep. So no reported number moves either way. The paper should still name it, because the reader cannot see that it does not matter without doing this arithmetic, and it would matter immediately for a faster scheme or a lower f_s.

blockers.object_or_step: What object is uniformized, and at what rate
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "Ground truth is generated by exact simulation of the continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) by uniformization, so the interval average of the conductance is realised from an actual sampled trajectory rather than from any moment-closure approximation. Uniformization draws the transition times themselves, so there is no within-interval discretisation to choose and none to justify." Theory: "each of which behaves as an independent continuous-time Markov chain over a small set of conformational states."
blockers.what_you_still_need: Whether the uniformized chain is the K=2 single-channel generator run N_ch times independently or the aggregated population birth-death chain on the number of open channels; the uniformization rate Lambda; and whether Lambda is reset at the concentration jumps, where the diagonal of Q changes (q_CC is 0 at 0 uM and -100 at 10 uM). Also, "draws the transition times themselves" describes Gillespie more naturally than uniformization, where the Poisson clock also emits self-transitions, so I cannot tell from the sentence which of the two is meant.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Per channel, Lambda = max_i |q_ii| = 100 s^-1, which happens to be the same in both segments, embedded chain I + Q/Lambda, event times uniform within the segment. Both readings and any admissible Lambda are exact and give the same law, so correctness is safe. What is not safe is my ability to say I implemented the paper's simulator rather than an equivalent one, which is the difference between a check and a coincidence if my numbers ever disagree.

blockers.object_or_step: Whether the seven acquisition intervals within a cell share one set of trajectories or get seven independent ensembles
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "Every maximum-likelihood grid cell reported here, the least-squares arm included, used $10^4$ recordings". Figure 4 caption: "Ten thousand recordings are simulated at every cell of the grid and scored by each member of the cost ladder." Figure 3: "One common set of a thousand recordings at the same cell ... is scored interval by interval by each member, with no fitting involved." The common-set statement is made for the four members at one cell and for nothing else.
blockers.what_you_still_need: Whether one continuous-time trajectory is binned seven ways (all seven Delta are multiples of the 20 us raw grid, so this is natural and cheap) or seven ensembles are drawn, and in the first case whether the instrumental noise is redrawn per binning or the raw noise is binned along with the signal. Also whether the least-squares arm and the macroscopic members share an ensemble on the grid; Methods says they are "written by different producers, so their output files carry different prefixes", which suggests separate runs.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Independent ensembles per (cell, interval) and separate ensembles for the least-squares arm, since the two arms are dispatched by different scripts. If it is actually one trajectory binned seven ways, the seven points along the interval axis of every panel are correlated, the interval axis is smoother than independent sampling would make it, and any bootstrap interval on a difference between two intervals is wrong.

blockers.object_or_step: The time stamp of a recorded value relative to its averaging window
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Theory writes the window as trailing: "$\bar{y}_t = \frac{1}{\Delta}\int_{t-\Delta}^{t} y(\tau)\,\mathrm{d}\tau$". Methods says only "Each recorded measurement is the mean of $n_{\mathrm{samp},t}$ consecutive raw samples". Appendix 1, for the av=0 members, uses the midpoint: "the observation is treated as an instantaneous sample taken at the centre of the window: the occupancy is propagated there first, by $\mathbf{P}(\Delta/2)$".
blockers.what_you_still_need: Whether a recorded sample is plotted and indexed at the start, the centre or the end of its window. It does not change the likelihood, and the protocol segments align with interval boundaries so it does not shift the jump, but it shifts every trace by up to one interval against the protocol.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Indexed at the end of the window, following Theory's trailing integral. Wrong only costs a half-interval or one-interval shift in any figure where a trace is drawn against time.

blockers.object_or_step: Unitary conductance against unitary current, and the absence of a driving force
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "a unitary conductance $g$ set to $1$ (the engine parameter \texttt{unitary\_current}, written $i$ where the noise axis is defined below), and a current baseline $b$ set to $1$ (both in units of $g$)" and "Current is expressed throughout in units of the unitary conductance $g$, which corresponds physically to a single-channel current of roughly $1\;\mathrm{pA}$." Theory: "A channel in state $k$ carries a conductance $\gamma_k$".
blockers.what_you_still_need: Nothing that stops me, but the paper uses one symbol for a conductance and a current and never names a holding potential or a driving force, so a current is being expressed in units of a conductance. There is also a second naming hazard: Figure 2's caption calls the swept noise parameter "$\log_{10}\sigma$" where "$\sigma$ is the instrumental noise level ... with a simulated value of $10^{-4}$", which is Current_Noise, a variance density in g^2 s, and not a standard deviation. A reader who takes the symbol at face value is off by a square root and by a factor of the interval.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: The driving force is folded into the unitary current and set to 1, so gamma_O = i = g = 1 and every current in the paper is a dimensionless multiple of the single-channel current. That is consistent with the noise conversion, which uses i^2 in the denominator of S_tilde and gives S_tilde = label/10 at the run values, so it checks out. Nothing breaks if I take it this way.

got_through:
I wrote all seven members from the paper alone (Python, K=2, states C/O), plus an exact per-channel Gillespie simulator, and ran them at the paper's reference cell (N_ch=100, Current_Noise=1e-4, Delta=1 ms, 100 intervals split 20:40:40, 300 recordings).

What worked. The van Loan block construction (Eq. augmented) gives F1, F2 and hence Gammabar, Vbar, gbar0, G and H directly; the propagation and update (Eqs. mu-prop, sig-prop, mu-post, sig-post) are unambiguous; the three switches of Appendix 1 do fix the six lattice members, and the LSE recipe of Appendix 1 fixes the seventh. I confirmed my reading of the av=1 tilde by reproducing the paper's own MR/IR identity (Eq. mr-ir-identity) to 1e-16 numerically, which is the only thing in the paper that pins which covariance (Sigma_0, un-reduced, start frame) enters the av=1 quadratic form and gain.

Numbers, mine against the paper's ensemble-mean total log-likelihood (04_results.tex): LSE -262.3 +/- 1.3 against -262 +/- 0.73; R -146.8 +/- 0.4 against -147 +/- 0.20; IR -142.8 +/- 0.4 against -143 +/- 0.24. Mean squared standardized residual: R 0.773 against the Fig. 3 caption's 0.782; IR 0.984 against "one"; INR 0.990 against 0.9995. So four of the seven reproduce, and I take that as evidence the rest of my reading (per-channel moment convention, e_t = Current_Noise/Delta, Sigma_init = 0, Gaussian per-interval term with the 2*pi constant, prediction of interval 1 from the initial condition) is right.

(2) NR does not reproduce. (3) The binomial-count floor of 5 has no scope, and read literally it would demote R/MR/VR/IR to non-recursive over roughly half of every recording at this cell (N_ch*mu_O is 0 through the whole 20-interval pre-pulse and back below 5 about 30 ms into the washout). blockers.object_or_step: The mean trust coefficient alpha_mu: the constants c and epsilon of the smooth form, and the definition of alpha_p
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: "An undamped Kalman-like update can drive entries of $\bm{\mu}$ negative or above one, so the mean step is scaled by a trust coefficient $\alpha_\mu\in(0,1]$, the largest scaling that keeps the posterior on the simplex." and "The coefficient is therefore taken in the smooth form $\alpha = \tfrac12\bigl(1 + c\,\alpha_p - \sqrt{(1-c\,\alpha_p)^2+\epsilon^2}\bigr)$, which is a softened minimum and is infinitely differentiable in $\bm{\theta}$ everywhere. Reimplementing it with a hard minimum reproduces the mean current and corrupts every quantity this paper measures." (06_methods.tex)
blockers.what_you_still_need: The numerical values of c and epsilon, and the definition of alpha_p as a formula. "The largest scaling that keeps the posterior on the simplex" is a description of a hard bound, not of alpha_p: it does not say whether alpha_p is that bound itself, or that bound divided by the step, or the reciprocal, and c*alpha_p has to be a pure number of order one for the softmin to make sense. I also need to know whether alpha_mu multiplies the whole increment g*delta/sigma^2 or is applied per state, and whether the innovation used in the log-likelihood is the undamped one. The paper states the damping matters for the derivative, and this paper differentiates the log-likelihood, so getting c and epsilon wrong changes the score and every diagnostic downstream, not just a few intervals.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: alpha_p = the largest scalar in (0,1] with mu_prop + alpha_p*step inside [0,1]^K, c = 1, epsilon = 1e-6, applied to the whole increment, with the undamped innovation in the log-likelihood. Measured with a plain hard minimum instead (alpha = alpha_p): all failures disappear at every channel count I tried, and the ensemble-mean log-likelihood moves by 0.05 to 0.8 nats (N_ch=10: R -80.62 broken to -79.85; N_ch=100: IR -143.42 to -143.37). So the guess costs little on the log-likelihood and, by the paper's own sentence, corrupts the score and the Fisher information, which are the quantities the paper is about.

blockers.object_or_step: The non-recursive instantaneous member NR (av=0, recursion off): which frame the observation is predicted in, and what predictive variance it carries

got_through:
I read the nine .tex files and reconstructed the classical arm as far as the paper allows. What I could pin down:

TWO CONFIGURATIONS, both "family approximation = 2", data key nonlinearsqr, non-recursive, averaging flag 1, variance flag ignored (Methods, "The two least-squares configurations").

(1) SIX-PARAMETER, file figure_3_time_LSE.macroir. All six free in log10: k_on, k_off, unitary current, Current_Noise, baseline, mean channel number. Two directions are flat by construction: Current_Noise has an identically zero score row and zero Fisher row, and (unitary current, N_ch) is a rank-one degenerate block along the amplitude ridge N_ch*i. No fitting is done under it; it only scores. Used for Figure 3 and its two supplements.

(2) FOUR-PARAMETER, files figure_4_LSE.macroir (grid) and figure_3_mle_LSE.macroir (same model, per-group MLE cloud retained). Unitary current fixed at 1 and Current_Noise fixed at the cell value, both equal to the simulated truth by construction (one parameter vector is passed to the simulator and to the fit). Free: k_on, k_off, baseline, N_ch, indices 0..3 with index 2 = baseline and no unitary-current index. Used for Figures 4 and 6, and (by inference, not by statement) Figure 2.

WHAT IS MINIMISED. The sum of squared residuals between the recorded interval averages and the deterministic mean current, with the mean built as in the Appendix: propagate the occupancy alone, mu_prop = P(Delta)^T mu_0, no covariance and no update, and predict ybar = N_ch * mu_0^T gammabar_0 (+ baseline, per Methods). Because averaging = 1, the conductance is the start-conditioned interval-averaged gammabar_0 of Eq. gammabar, not the instantaneous gamma, so the F_1 van Loan block is needed even for least squares. Both configurations minimise the same sum of squares, so the free/fixed split does not change the objective's form.

RESIDUAL VARIANCE. One constant sigma-hat^2 for the whole record, "estimated as the residual sum of squares over the record" (Results) / "over the number of samples" (Appendix). Since a constant weight does not move the argmin, the fit is well defined either way, but every downstream number divides by this constant.

FISHER. Eq. gaussian-fisher with sigma_t^2 replaced by one constant sigma^2. The variance-derivative term (grad sigma^2)(grad sigma^2)^T / (2 sigma^4) vanishes identically, because the constant does not depend on any parameter; that is the same fact as the zero Current_Noise Fisher row. So H_LSE = sum_t (grad mu_t)(grad mu_t)^T / sigma^2, which is the classical Gauss-Newton normal matrix. It differs from the members' in exactly two ways: no variance channel (which is why it cannot separate i from N_ch, and why the amplitude and noise panels of Figure 2 are empty by construction), and the dimension, 4x4 against the members' 6x6, so no eigenvalue-accumulating scalar is comparable across arms.

CONFIDENCE INTERVAL. Reported covariance = H^{-1} of the Gaussian-Fisher family evaluated at theta_pool, scaled by the reciprocal of the group size (Figure 2 caption). Corrected covariance = sandwich H^{-1} J H^{-1}, with J the across-replicate covariance of the total score and bootstrap percentile intervals over groups, B = 100. No (n-p) correction and no t quantile are mentioned anywhere.

CROSS-CHECK I RAN. Back-solving the reported LSE log-likelihood at the reference cell (N_ch 100, label 0.1, Delta*k_off 0.1, so n = 100 intervals) under the concentrated Gaussian form ell = -(n/2)log(2 pi sigma-hat^2) - n/2 gives sigma-hat^2 = 11.0 for ell = -262. That is the right order for the record-averaged total variance at that cell (about 23 during the plateau, 0.1 in the pre-pulse, decaying in the post-pulse), and it is consistent with the quoted per-step median log10(J_t/F_t) = +0.184, i.e. a true-over-assumed variance ratio of 1.53 at the informative steps, and with 14.96/1.53 = 9.8 against the quoted residual integrated autocorrelation of 9.26. So the plug-in-SSE reading hangs together. None of this is stated; I had to back-solve it from a reported number, which is not a verification.
stopped_at: The first thing I could not do was give the constant sigma^2 a number. The objective's argmin does not need it, but the score, the reported Fisher, the reported interval, the sandwich and the whole 13-to-15-fold LSE distortion all divide by it, and the distortion scales as 1/sigma^2 exactly. The paper supplies two mutually exclusive readings of what that constant is (a plug-in fitted from the residuals, or the Current_Noise the four-parameter configuration fixes at the cell value), and they differ by more than a factor of a hundred at the reference cell. I assumed the plug-in reading and carried on, and then hit the second wall at the LSE score and log-likelihood, neither of which is written anywhere in the nine files, and the third at Figure 3, whose anchor parameter vector is never named.

blockers.object_or_step: The single constant residual variance sigma^2 that LSE's score, Fisher, interval and distortion all divide by
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Appendix 1: "assigns one constant variance to every residual, fitted as the residual sum of squares over the number of samples." Results: "assigns one constant variance $\hat\sigma^2$ to every residual, estimated as the residual sum of squares over the record." Against Methods: "Both fix the unitary current at $1$ and \texttt{Current\_Noise} at the cell value, leaving four free parameters" and "Both fixed values are the values the recordings were simulated from." Diagnostics only says "$\mathbf{H}$ as written above with $\sigma_t^2$ replaced by one constant $\sigma^2$" and never says which constant.

Reading "samples" as raw samples puts sigma-hat^2 out by a factor of 50 and the log-likelihood out by a factor of 50 in n.

blockers.object_or_step: Whether the LSE column of Figure 3 is scored on the same recordings as the macroscopic columns
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Results: "One common set of a thousand recordings at the same cell ... is scored interval by interval by each member, with no fitting involved." Against Methods: "LSE and the macroscopic members are written by different producers, so their output files carry different prefixes", and "The simulation seed was set to $0$, which in this engine is the sentinel for a random seed drawn from \texttt{std::random\_device}, and the resolved seed was never logged."
blockers.what_you_still_need: Whether the two producers ran in one process on one realised ensemble, or on two independent draws that are only statistically equivalent. With an unlogged random seed, two producers cannot share an ensemble unless they ran together.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Two independent draws. That is fine for the ensemble means but it means -262 against -230 is not a paired comparison on the same data, and the standard errors quoted (0.73, 0.83) understate the uncertainty of the difference relative to a paired reading of the same sentence.

blockers.object_or_step: The anchor (theta_sim or theta_pool) at which Figure 3 and its supplements are evaluated
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Diagnostics: "Everything below is computed at both anchors and every figure states which one it shows". Figure 3's caption states no anchor: "One set of $1{,}000$ recordings ($N_{\mathrm{ch}}=100$, noise label $0.1$, $\Delta\!\cdot\!k_{\mathrm{off}}=0.1$) is scored by each of the seven members (columns, in cost-ladder order), with no fitting."
blockers.what_you_still_need: The anchor. Every LSE number in that subsection depends on it: -262 nats, the accumulated ratio 14.96, the per-step median +0.184, the lag-one score autocorrelation 0.856.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: theta_sim, because row D is "the mean per-interval score over $\sqrt{F_t}$, zero when unbiased", which is only a meaningful display at the truth, and because no fitting was done. If it is theta_pool instead, the six-parameter LSE has no theta_pool at all, since two of its directions are flat and the pooled fit is not defined.

blockers.object_or_step: The mask that defines an "informative step" for the per-interval medians
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Results: "the median of $\log_{10}(J_t/F_t)$ over the informative steps is $+0.184$ for \texttt{LSE}". Figure 3 caption: "curves stop where the information reaches zero." No numerical threshold is given for F_t anywhere; the only tolerance in the paper, $\lambda_i > \lambda_{\max}\cdot 10^{-10}$, is stated for the eigenmodes of the matrix anchor H, not for the per-interval scalar.
blockers.what_you_still_need: The rule: an absolute floor on F_t, a fraction of the peak F_t, or the same relative eigenvalue tolerance applied per interval.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: An absolute floor of about 1e-6 on F_t. The median is quoted to six decimals (0.183889), and the value of a median over a masked set moves with the mask, so a different rule changes the sixth decimal and can change the second.

blockers.object_or_step: The LSE mean model: interval-averaged or instantaneous conductance, and where the baseline and the sign flip enter
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Theory Table 1 puts LSE at "the fluctuations are not modelled ... the deterministic mean current only". Methods: "it runs non-recursive with the averaging flag at $1$". Appendix: "predicts $\bar{y}^{\mathrm{pred}}$ from Eq.~\ref{eq:ypred}", which is $\bar{y}^{\mathrm{pred}} = N_{\mathrm{ch}}\,\bm{\mu}_0^\top \bar{\bm{\gamma}}_0$ with no baseline. Methods separately gives "$\bar y_t = N_{\mathrm{ch}}\,\mu_t\!\cdot\!\gamma_t + b$" and "the code applies a sign flip so the single-channel current is inward".
blockers.what_you_still_need: Confirmation that av=1 means LSE's mean uses the start-conditioned interval average gammabar_0 (so that a least-squares implementation needs the van Loan F_1 block), and an explicit statement of whether the baseline is added before or after the sign flip.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: ybar_t = b - N_ch * mu_t^T gammabar_0(Delta), with gamma = (0, i) and the sign flip applied to the channel term only. Getting the averaging wrong (using instantaneous gamma) matters at the coarse end of the interval sweep, which is exactly where Figure 6's ribbons run to Delta*k_off = 1; getting the sign convention wrong flips the sign of the baseline estimate and of the score rows.

blockers.object_or_step: Whether the expectation in the Gaussian Fisher is taken over the ensemble for LSE
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Diagnostics gives $\mathbf{H}=\sum_t\mathbb{E}[\cdot]$; Methods gives "$\bar G = \sum_t \mathrm{GFI}_t$" and says "which follows from the analytic derivative alone and needs no extra likelihood passes."
blockers.what_you_still_need: For a member whose sigma^2 is estimated from the data, GFI_t is a random variable per recording. The paper does not say whether H is computed per recording and averaged, computed once from an ensemble-averaged sigma-hat^2, or computed at the pooled fit only.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Per recording, then averaged over the ensemble. The difference is O(1/n) on the mean but it changes the bootstrap interval on the LSE ratio, and the paper quotes that interval (13.86 to 15.93).

blockers.object_or_step: How the reported confidence interval is formed from an LSE fit
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Figure 2 caption: "Covariances are the Gaussian-Fisher family at the pooled estimate, scaled by the reciprocal of the group size." Nothing states an (n-p) correction, a t quantile, or whether the classical arm's interval is the one a standard curve-fitting package would report.
blockers.what_you_still_need: An explicit statement that the classical interval under test is the plain Fisher-based normal interval sigma-hat^2 (J^T J)^{-1} with divisor n, and not the textbook sigma-hat^2 = SSE/(n-p) with a t quantile. The paper's headline claim is about "the classical error bar", so which classical error bar is load-bearing.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Plain normal interval, divisor n, no t quantile, covariance for a group of g recordings taken as H_single^{-1}/g at theta_pool. If the intended target is the textbook interval, the reported distortion should be scaled by (n-p)/n and the quoted 11.79/13.06/13.04/12.97 all move by a few percent.

blockers.object_or_step: Which least-squares configuration produces Figure 2
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods names only two figures: "This is the configuration behind every least-squares cell of Figures~4 and~6." Figure 2 is not named there. Results says of Figure 2's LSE column: "Its grid configuration holds the unitary current and the instrumental noise level fixed at the values the recordings were simulated from (Methods)".
blockers.what_you_still_need: One word in the Methods sentence. It is recoverable, since figure_3_mle_LSE.macroir is described as the four-parameter model "run with the per-group estimate cloud retained", and Figure 2 is the cloud figure.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: The four-parameter configuration. If it were the six-parameter one, the quoted LSE ratios 14.78 and 1.63 would be 6x6 objects and not comparable with the other members' as the figure presents them.

blockers.object_or_step: Which configuration produces the LSE curves in Figure 1 and in Figure 4 supplements 8 and 9
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Nothing. Figure 1's caption says only "\texttt{LSE} is drawn in \texttt{NR}'s grammar, a point mean with an error bar" and that the trace is "one $20$-channel trace simulated with $250$ within-interval substeps". The residual integrated autocorrelation of 9.26 is attributed to "figure_4_supplement_8" with no configuration named.
blockers.what_you_still_need: For Figure 1, the parameter vector at which the LSE mean and its SSE are computed, and whether the SSE is over the whole 12 ms record or the 4 ms window shown. For supplement 9 (the score autocorrelation over the plane), the configuration, since which score rows exist depends on it.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Figure 1 at the simulation truth with SSE over the whole record; supplements 8 and 9 on the four-parameter grid lane. The residual autocorrelation is insensitive to the free/fixed split at fixed theta, so 9.26 is probably reproducible either way; the score autocorrelation is not.

blockers.object_or_step: The noise levels at which the least-squares grid was actually run
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: "the least-squares arm covers $30$ cells on $N_{\mathrm{ch}} \in \{10, 100, 1000, 10000\}$, with labels from $0.1$ up to $10^4$, $10^5$, $10^6$ and $10^7$ respectively." The intermediate labels are never listed for this arm; the IR sweep is separately said to run "noise labels from $0.05$ to $10^6$".
blockers.what_you_still_need: The label list. Figure 6's least-squares boundaries are fitted through four measured crossings, so where the crossings fall depends on which labels bracket them.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Whole decades from 0.1, giving 6, 7, 8 and 9 labels at the four channel counts, which sums to exactly 30. That arithmetic is a good sign but it excludes the 0.05, 0.2 and 0.5 levels the IR sweep carries, so an LSE crossing quoted at 164 in label units is interpolated between decade points, not measured at one.

blockers.object_or_step: The "distortion-corrected standard error crosses a factor of two" boundary, which Figure 6 takes for the rates from the least-squares arm
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Figure 6 caption: "solid asks whether the parameter can be measured at all, drawn where the distortion-corrected standard error crosses a factor of two". Results: "The rate boundaries are taken from the least-squares arm and the amplitude boundaries from the likelihood".
blockers.what_you_still_need: The sample size the standard error refers to (one recording, one group of ten, or the pooled 10^4) and the units (parameters are fitted in log10, so "a factor of two" presumably means SE = log10(2) = 0.301 in log10 units). Neither is stated.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: One recording, SE = 0.301 in log10 units, taken as the square root of the diagonal of H^{-1} J H^{-1}. Getting the sample size wrong shifts every solid boundary by a factor of sqrt(10) or 100 in the standard error, which moves the reachability floors (17 channels for N_ch, 52 for k_on) and the region-3 opening range (120 to 1368) by decades.

blockers.object_or_step: Whether Current_Noise is a free parameter of the six-parameter least-squares fit
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "All six parameters are free in base-ten logarithmic coordinates: $k_{\mathrm{on}}$, $k_{\mathrm{off}}$, the unitary current, \texttt{Current\_Noise}, the current baseline and the mean channel number", and then "\texttt{Current\_Noise} has an identically zero score row and an identically zero Fisher row". Results: "least squares has no score in that direction at all, because its noise level is a plug-in from the same record rather than a free parameter."
blockers.what_you_still_need: A statement that Current_Noise is declared free for index alignment with the macroscopic dumps but does not enter the objective, so "free" here is a bookkeeping status and not an estimated parameter. As written the two sentences contradict each other.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Declared free, inert in the objective. This is only a reader's trap, not a numerical one, but it cost me a pass to resolve and it is what makes the four-parameter configuration's "Current_Noise fixed at the cell value" a no-op rather than a modelling choice.

blockers.object_or_step: The fixed unitary current as it enters the conductance vector
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "a unitary conductance $g$ set to $1$ (the engine parameter \texttt{unitary\_current}, written $i$ where the noise axis is defined below)" and "Only the open state conducts, and the code applies a sign flip so the single-channel current is inward."
blockers.what_you_still_need: Confirmation that gamma = (0, i) for the closed and open states with the sign carried separately, and that "fix the unitary current at 1" means i = 1 in the same units the current is expressed in (units of g), so that the fixed value and the scale of the current are the same number.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: gamma = (0, 1) with an overall sign flip on the channel term. If instead the sign is folded into gamma, the amplitude ridge N_ch*i has the opposite sign and the LSE baseline estimate absorbs it, which would show up as a baseline bias I could not attribute.

got_through:
I could write down most of the design skeleton from Methods, and it is internally consistent where it is given.

INTERVAL AXIS (complete and checkable). Seven levels of Delta/tau = 1, 0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01, realised as 500/250/100/50/25/10/5 raw samples at f_s = 50 kHz, i.e. 10/5/2/1/0.5/0.2/0.1 ms, giving 10/20/50/100/200/500/1000 steps in a record of fixed total duration 100 ms, split 20:40:40 into pre-pulse (0 uM), agonist (10 uM) and post-pulse (0 uM). I checked this: 0.02 ms per raw sample x 500 = 10 ms = tau = 1/k_off, and every step count is divisible by 5 so the segment ratio always lands on integers. Consistent.

TRUTH AND PARAMETERISATION. Two states C/O, only O conducts, all channels closed at t=0 so occupancy is (1,0); six parameters, all in log10: k_on = 10 /uM/s, k_off = 100 /s, unitary conductance g = 1, baseline b = 1, plus the swept Current_Noise and mean channel number. k_on[A] = 100 /s at 10 uM against k_off = 100 /s gives P_open = 0.5, matching the Introduction. Noise label = 1000 x Current_Noise, dimensionless S~ = label/10; label 0.1 is Current_Noise = 1e-4, which matches the "simulated value of 1e-4" for log10 sigma in Figure 2. Emission: ybar = N_ch mu.gamma + b, sigma^2 = e_t + N_ch v_t with e_t = Current_Noise/Delta_t. I can implement all of that.

CHANNEL COUNTS. IR at {5,10,20,50,100,200,500,1000,2000,5000,10000}; NR at {10,100,1000,10000}; R at those plus 5, 20, 50 at label 0.1; MR/VR at "the same channel numbers" at labels {0.1, 1, 10}; LSE at {10,100,1000,10000} on 30 cells.

ENSEMBLE SIZE. 10^4 recordings for every maximum-likelihood grid cell including LSE; 1,000 recordings for the time-resolved run; Figure 1 is one 20-channel trace from a different (substep) sampler and does not enter any comparison.

GROUPING. Partition by position into consecutive groups, remainder dropped; group sizes 10 and 100; 10^4 recordings give 1,000 groups of 10 or 100 groups of 100. Figure 2 is the group-of-10 case at N_ch=100, label 0.1, Delta*k_off=0.1.

FITTED VS SCORED. Fitted: the per-group MLE cloud (only on the lane that keeps that stage) and the pooled joint fit over all 10^4 at once, per member per cell; likelihood members free in all six parameters, LSE free in four (k_on, k_off, baseline, N_ch; unitary current and Current_Noise fixed at their simulated values, indices 0/1/2/3 with index 2 the baseline) for Figures 4 and 6, and free in all six for the time-resolved figure. Only scored, no fitting: the 1,000-recording time-resolved run of Figure 3.

ANCHORS. theta_sim = the simulation truth; theta_pool = the joint MLE over all replicates of one cell, located by Gauss-Newton with Levenberg damping warm-started at the truth, accepted on a near-zero gradient. Figure 4A uses theta_sim, Figure 4B and Figure 5 use theta_pool, Figure 2's reported covariance is the Gaussian Fisher at theta_pool scaled by 1/group size.

OPTIMISER. Gauss-Newton + Levenberg, warm start at truth, initial damping 10, growth factor 3, max damping 1e10, at most 100 iterations, relative gradient tolerance 1e-6 (taken relative to the warm-start norm), value tolerance 1e-10, with the operative criterion a Newton decrement 0.5 g'H^-1 g below 1e-8 for the first ten iterations and below 1e-4 after.

I also checked the stated grid against the stated tallies and found the coverage is reconstructable for NR and MR but not for R or IR: with 4 parameters per cell and 7 intervals per (N_ch, label) pair, NR's 896 points give exactly 224 cells = 32 pairs x 7, MR's 336 give 84 = 12 pairs x 7 = 4 counts x 3 labels x 7, and R's 980 give 245 = 35 pairs x 7 = NR's 32 pairs plus exactly the 3 extra counts at label 0.1 that Methods names. That is a strong enough agreement that I believe NR and R carry 8 noise labels at each of their four channel counts. LSE's "30 cells" is exactly 6+7+8+9, i.e. decade labels 0.1 up to 1e4/1e5/1e6/1e7. Those two facts are the only handle I have on the noise axis, and they are not enough (see blockers).
stopped_at: I stopped at instantiating the noise axis. Methods gives ranges ("noise labels from 0.05 to 10^6") but never lists the levels, and the paper's own two counts of them disagree (Results says eleven noise levels, Discussion says twelve), so I cannot write the grid down, cannot say which cells exist for any member, and cannot check my cell set against the paper's tallies. Assuming decade spacing from 0.05 (which reproduces LSE's 30 cells but gives 9 levels, not 11 or 12) and carrying on, the next hard stops were, in order: the two contradictory definitions of the constant variance that least squares reports; the undetermined constants c and epsilon in the smooth trust coefficient, which Methods itself says are load-bearing; the coverage cell, which needs 10^5 recordings to give the thousand fits at group size 100 it reports while every cell is said to have 10^4; and the reference ensemble behind the "distortion-corrected standard error crosses a factor of two" boundary, which sets where the whole of Figure 6's reachability half sits and is never named.

blockers.object_or_step: The noise axis: which labels were actually run
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "Across the three directories, \texttt{IR} covers $N_{\mathrm{ch}} \in \{5, 10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000, 2000, 5000, 10000\}$ and noise labels from $0.05$ to $10^6$". Results: "the boundary-conditioned member spans eleven channel counts from $5$ to $10^4$ across eleven noise levels, not on a full rectangle". Discussion: "spanning eleven channel counts from $5$ to $10^4$ and twelve instrumental noise levels with seven acquisition intervals resolved inside each cell".
blockers.what_you_still_need: The explicit list of noise labels. Ranges plus a count are not enough, and the paper gives two different counts (eleven in Results, twelve in Discussion) for the same member.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Decades from 0.05: {0.05, 0.1, 1, 10, 1e2, 1e3, 1e4, 1e5, 1e6}. That reproduces the LSE arm exactly (6+7+8+9 = 30 cells) but gives nine levels, not eleven or twelve, so the guess is demonstrably incomplete: there are two or three intermediate labels I cannot name. Every cell-count, every 'fraction of the plane' statistic and every fitted boundary slope in Figure 6 is computed over a grid I cannot instantiate.

blockers.object_or_step: Which noise labels go with which channel count, per member
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "NR covers $N_{\mathrm{ch}} \in \{10, 100, 1000, 10000\}$ and R covers those and additionally $5$, $20$ and $50$ at label $0.1$, with the highest labels run only at the larger channel counts and reaching $10^7$ at $N_{\mathrm{ch}} = 10^4$".
blockers.what_you_still_need: The label set at each channel count. 'The highest labels run only at the larger channel counts' names no labels and no counts.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: From the tallies, 8 labels at each of the four channel counts for both NR and R (896/4/7 = 32 = 8 x 4; 980/4/7 = 35 = 32 + 3), with the window sliding upward with N_ch as it does for LSE: 0.05..1e3 at N_ch 10 through 0.1..1e7 at N_ch 1e4. If the window does not slide, or slides by a different amount, the noise-direction sequences quoted in Results (R at 1.42 / 1.03 / 1.00 across labels 0.1 / 100 / 1000 at N_ch 1e4) sit at cells that do not exist in my grid.

blockers.object_or_step: MR and VR coverage: the antecedent of 'the same channel numbers'
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "MR and VR cover the same channel numbers at labels $\{0.1, 1, 10\}$".
blockers.what_you_still_need: Whether 'the same' means NR's four counts or R's four-plus-three.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: NR's four, {10, 100, 1000, 10000}: 4 counts x 3 labels x 7 intervals x 4 parameters = 336, which is exactly the point count Results gives for the one-endpoint member ("$20\%$ ($67$ of $336$)"). I am fairly confident, but it is an inference from an arithmetic coincidence, not from a sentence.

blockers.object_or_step: INR's coverage on the design plane
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: The coverage paragraph of Methods lists IR, NR, R, MR, VR and the least-squares arm and never mentions INR. Table 1 caption says only: "INR is the member published as MacroINR in \citet{moffatt2025bayesian} ... it is reported here only in the supplement."
blockers.what_you_still_need: Which channel counts, noise labels and intervals INR was run at, if any beyond the single time-resolved cell of Figure 3. The Results tally sentence covers IR, R, NR and 'the one-endpoint member carried in the supplement' (336 points = MR or VR), so INR appears in no tally either.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: That INR was run only at the Figure 3 cell (N_ch=100, label 0.1, Delta*k_off=0.1) and nowhere on the plane. If it was in fact run on a grid, I have no way to reproduce the supplement that reports it, and the paper's own 'seven rungs, all implemented and measured' claim is one rung short on the plane.

blockers.object_or_step: Whether all seven acquisition intervals were run at every (member, N_ch, label) cell
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "The acquisition interval was swept over seven levels of $\Delta/\tau$" and, separately, "The label range is deliberately not rectangular: the highest noise labels were run only at the larger channel numbers." Results: "Taking the median over the seven intervals at noise label $0.1$". Nothing states the interval coverage per member or per cell.
blockers.what_you_still_need: A statement that the interval sweep is full inside every surviving (N_ch, label) pair, for every member including LSE.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Full: 7 intervals everywhere. The point counts are all divisible by 7 after dividing by 4 parameters, which supports it. If some cells carry fewer intervals, my medians over intervals (the numbers Results quotes for R, IR, NR and LSE) are taken over a different set than theirs.

blockers.object_or_step: The cell counts do not reconcile with the point counts, and 'cell' is used in two senses
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Results: "the reported uncertainty is within $\pm15\%$ of the delivered one for $93\%$ of the boundary-conditioned member's points ($2116$ of $2268$, over $560$ cells), $70\%$ of the recursive instantaneous member's ($684$ of $980$, over $238$ cells), and $31\%$ of the open-loop member's ($277$ of $896$, over $224$ cells)". Methods: "the least-squares arm covers $30$ cells on $N_{\mathrm{ch}} \in \{10, 100, 1000, 10000\}$".
blockers.what_you_still_need: A definition of 'cell' and one self-consistent set of counts. NR reconciles exactly (896 = 4 x 224), but IR gives 2268/4 = 567 against a stated 560, and R gives 980/4 = 245 against a stated 238: both short by exactly 7, i.e. one (N_ch,label) pair's worth of intervals. And LSE's '30 cells' can only be (N_ch,label) pairs, since 30 is 6+7+8+9 decade labels, while the 560/238/224 counts must include the interval.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: That 'cell' = (N_ch, label, Delta) in Results and (N_ch, label) in the LSE sentence, and that 560 and 238 are stale by one pair each. I cannot tell which of the two numbers in each pair is the right one, so I cannot say whether my reconstructed grid is missing seven cells or theirs has seven extra points.

blockers.object_or_step: Which parameters enter the +/-15% tallies
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Results: "Over the whole measured grid, counting every parameter at every cell, the reported uncertainty is within $\pm15\%$ ...". Elsewhere five are enumerated: "\texttt{R} departs on $0.4375$, $0.5625$, $0.2232$, $0.3125$ and $0.0000$ of the plane for $k_{\mathrm{on}}$, $k_{\mathrm{off}}$, $i$, $N_{\mathrm{ch}}$ and the noise level". Methods says the likelihood members' distortion matrix is $6\times 6$.
blockers.what_you_still_need: Which of the six directions are counted. 'Every parameter' cannot mean six (2268/6 = 378, and then R's 980 is not divisible by 6) and cannot mean five (2268/5 and 980/5 are not both integers with the stated cell counts); the counts only work at four per cell.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Four: k_on, k_off, i, N_ch, dropping the baseline and the instrumental noise level. But Results quotes the noise-level fraction explicitly as part of the same comparison, so the guess contradicts the text it is supposed to reproduce, and my 93% / 70% / 31% will not match theirs if I pick the wrong four.

blockers.object_or_step: Whether the channel count is fixed per recording or drawn
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods calls the swept parameter "the mean channel number" throughout: "while the white-noise level and the mean channel number were swept", and lists among the free parameters "the current baseline and the mean channel number". The emission is "$\bar y_t = N_{\mathrm{ch}}\,\mu_t\!\cdot\!\gamma_t + b$ and variance $\sigma_t^2 = e_t + N_{\mathrm{ch}}\,v_t$". No sentence says whether the count in a given simulated recording equals $N_{\mathrm{ch}}$ exactly.
blockers.what_you_still_need: One sentence saying the per-recording channel count is deterministic (or naming the distribution it is drawn from and whether the likelihood marginalises over it).
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Deterministic, exactly N_ch in every recording, because the predictive variance carries no term for a fluctuating count. If it is actually drawn (Poisson, say), the simulated ensemble has an extra between-recording variance that no member models, J is inflated for every member at once, and the whole distortion map shifts upward, which would be misread as a likelihood failure. The name of the parameter argues the other way from the formula, which is why I flag it.

blockers.object_or_step: The coverage cell (Figure 4 supplement 4/5): ensemble size and group count
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Results: "the nominal $95\%$ region of \texttt{IR} covers $0.914$ of the estimates under its own Fisher covariance and $0.947$ to $0.949$ under the sandwich, measured at $N_{\mathrm{ch}}=10$ and noise label $0.05$ over a thousand fits in six parameters at group size $100$". Against Methods: "Every maximum-likelihood grid cell reported here, the least-squares arm included, used $10^4$ recordings" and "Two group sizes were used, $10$ and $100$; with $10{,}000$ recordings these give $1{,}000$ groups of $10$ and $100$ groups of $100$."
blockers.what_you_still_need: Resolution: a thousand fits at group size 100 needs 10^5 recordings, five times what every cell is said to have. Either that cell was run at 10^5, or the group size is 10, or 'a thousand fits' is wrong.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: That the cell was run at 10^5 recordings and is an exception to the 10^4 rule. If instead it was 100 fits at group size 100, the coverage estimate 0.914 has a binomial standard error near 0.03 rather than 0.009, and the 0.914-vs-0.947 separation I am trying to reproduce is inside noise.

blockers.object_or_step: Which cells get a per-group MLE cloud, and at which group size
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods: "On the grid-production lane the cloud stage and the capstone are dropped, because no map reads them there; the cells that need a cloud are produced by the separate script that keeps that stage." And: "Two group sizes were used, $10$ and $100$".
blockers.what_you_still_need: The list of cells that carry a cloud, and which group size each uses. Only two cloud cells are identifiable from the text (N_ch=100/label 0.1 at group size 10 for Figure 2; N_ch=10/label 0.05 at group size 100 for the coverage supplement), and the rule that decides the group size is never given.
blockers.what_you_would_guess: Group size 10 at the well-determined cells and 100 where the per-group fit would not converge at 10 recordings (few channels). If I pick the wrong size, the empirical cloud covariance scales by 10 and every ellipse-area ratio in Figure 2 moves by that factor, since the reported covariance is explicitly 'scaled by the reciprocal of the group size'.

blockers.object_or_step: The anchor for Figure 3 and Figure 6
blockers.what_the_paper_gives_you: Methods promises: "Every diagnostic below is computed at both anchors ... Each figure states which anchor it uses." got_through:
I got the whole algebraic skeleton of the diagnostic written down, and for the two non-recursive members (NR, INR) I could code it end to end.

What the paper hands over cleanly, and what I would have implemented:
- Score. S(theta) = grad ell(theta), total per recording, in base-ten log coordinates (Methods: "all estimated in base-ten logarithmic coordinates"). For a non-recursive member ell = sum_t log m_t(ybar_t) so s_t = grad log m_t and S = sum_t s_t; for a recursive member ell = sum_t log q_t(ybar_t | ybar_{1:t-1}) (Theory) so s_t is the gradient of the t-th prequential term and S = sum_t s_t exactly. Methods says the score is obtained by automatic differentiation, so I would tape the whole filter cycle of Appendix 1 and differentiate through the recursion.
- Reported information. H = sum_t GFI_t with GFI_t = (grad mu_t)(grad mu_t)^T / sigma_t^2 + (grad sigma_t^2)(grad sigma_t^2)^T / (2 sigma_t^4), written out identically in Diagnostics Eq. gaussian-fisher and in Methods. Per-interval F_t is its diagonal entry for the parameter under discussion and H_ii = sum_t F_t.
- Score covariance. J = Cov(S) across the M independent recordings of one design cell, cross-interval terms included; M = 10^4 for the grid cells and 1,000 for the time-resolved figure (Methods gives both).
- Distortion. C = H^(-1/2) J H^(-1/2), with H^(-1/2) the symmetric inverse root taken on the subspace of eigenmodes with lambda_i > lambda_max * 1e-10; undefined (not zero, rendered grey) when that subspace is empty. Direction convention is stated outright: C_ii > 1 is over-confidence, C_ii < 1 conservatism. Nothing to guess here.
- Split. J_s = sum_t Cov(s_t), C_s = H^(-1/2) J_s H^(-1/2) (per-sample), R = J_s^(-1/2) J J_s^(-1/2) (correlation/accumulated), with the exact composition C = K R K^T, K = H^(-1/2) J_s^(1/2), and log det C = log det C_s + log det R. Also kappa = Var(sum_t X_t) / sum_t Var(X_t) and T_eff = T/kappa.
- Scalars. m = exp(mean_i log lambda_i), a = exp(s) with s^2 = Var_i(log lambda_i), on the d retained eigenvalues of C. The paper's own identity D_AI = sqrt(sum_i log^2 lambda_i) = sqrt(d(ebar^2 + s^2)) pins Var_i to the population form (divide by d, not d-1), so that one potential ambiguity is closed by the text and I did not have to guess it.
- Sandwich and bias. Sigma = H^(-1) J H^(-1) = H^(-1/2) C H^(-1/2); b = H^(-1) E[S] evaluated at theta_sim; for the Figure 2 ellipse comparison the covariances are scaled by the reciprocal of the group size, which the caption states.
- Bootstrap counts. 100 replicates for the diagnostic battery, 200 for the empirical-versus-theoretical capstone, percentile intervals at 2.5/16/50/84/97.5 with no probit transform, verified equal to R quantile type 6. Maximum lag 10 for the score autocorrelation.
- Two anchors. theta_sim and theta_pool, every quantity computed at both, each figure naming which.

So the matrix algebra is complete and I would have coded C, C_s, R, m, a, D_AI, Sigma and b in an afternoon.
stopped_at:
I stopped hard at the score itself for the four recursive members (R, MR, VR, IR), which is the first object the diagnostic needs and the one every later quantity is built from. The paper says the filter carries a smooth trust coefficient alpha = (1/2)(1 + c*alpha_p - sqrt((1 - c*alpha_p)^2 + eps^2)) and then never gives c, never gives eps, and never defines alpha_p (it defines alpha_mu, a different symbol). It also says in the same paragraph that getting this wrong "corrupts every quantity this paper measures", so I cannot shrug and pick numbers. The companion safeguard, the binomial-count floor of 5, is given as a number with no rule: which count, tested against which state, for that interval or for the rest of the record, and how a hard fallback from recursive to non-recursive is differentiated inside an automatically differentiated recursion. Without both I cannot produce a score for the members the paper's headline results are about.

Assuming values for those, I carried on and hit a second class of blocker that is more damaging because it is silent: the reduction rules. Every headline number in the paper is a median, a fraction, an autocorrelation or an interval taken over some retained set of intervals or some resampling unit, and the paper names none of them. There is no definition of "the informative steps" or of "the information mask" over which the per-step medians (+0.184 / -0.038 / -0.181 / +0.006) are taken; no convention for the score autocorrelation on a series whose per-interval information spans forty decades within one record; no formula or truncation for the integrated autocorrelation quoted as 9.26 / 3.93 / 1.30 / 1.008; and Methods and the figure captions contradict each other on whether the bootstrap resamples groups or recordings, which is a factor of a hundred in the resampling unit and therefore in every interval width the paper prints.

And I stopped at the estimation floor, which the task named and which appears nowhere in the nine files. With M recordings and d parameters, sampling noise in J alone spreads the eigenvalues of C and pushes the anisotropy a above 1 even when the likelihood is perfectly specified. The paper reports distortions of 1.00, 1.01, 1.05, 0.998 and counts a point as calibrated at a 15 percent threshold, so the floor is of the same order as the effects being reported, and there is not one sentence about it. The closest the text comes is "the confidence interval narrows as the number of simulated recordings grows", which is a direction and not a floor. I could build my own null by drawing S ~ N(0, H) M times and re-estimating (m, a), but that gives me my floor, not theirs, so I cannot tell whether my C = 1.05 and their C = 1.05 are the same statement.

got_through:
I read the nine files and pulled 17 quoted results spanning Results and Discussion, then asked of each: are the conditions pinned, is the quantity defined, and can I put my number next to theirs.

WHAT I COULD ACTUALLY REPRODUCE (all of it internal arithmetic on the paper's own numbers, none of it a re-measurement):
- The fitted log-log slopes of the least-squares honesty boundary. Regressing the quoted crossings on log10 N_ch I get 1.006 (channel-number direction) and 1.026 (closing rate), against the quoted "slopes of 1.01 and 1.03". Reproduced.
- The error-bar translations. sqrt(1.15) = 1.072 -> 7%; sqrt(2) = 1.414 -> 41%; a distortion of 4 halves the interval and a nominal 95% interval covers 2*Phi(1.96/2)-1 = 0.673 -> "about 68%". All three reproduced exactly.
- The log-likelihood spread: -143 - (-262) = 119, quoted 118.9. And 10^(-3.667+4) = 2.15, quoted "a factor of 2.2 too much noise". Both reproduced.
- The joint four-parameter ellipse against the per-parameter distortion diagonal: sqrt(13.24*17.32*10.04*9.91) = 151.0 against the quoted 154.65 for NR. Consistent to 2%, which also tells me the joint number is sqrt(det) over the four informative directions.
- The coverage number is internally plausible: 0.914 coverage of a nominal 95% region in 6 degrees of freedom implies a uniform distortion of 1.137 (error bars 6.6% too narrow), which sits inside the IR distortions the paper quotes at N_ch = 10.
- The least-squares parameter-cancellation claim is verifiable analytically without any run: with s_t = (y_t - mu_t) grad mu_t / sigma^2 and a constant sigma^2, Var(s_t)/F_t = Var(y_t)/sigma^2, which carries no parameter, so "the same curve in all four bands ... median of 0.183889 in every one" is forced. That is the one claim in the paper I can certify from the text alone, and it is a good acceptance test for my own LSE arm.

WHAT WOULD NOT RECONCILE, on the paper's own numbers:
- 2268 measured points "one per parameter per design cell over 560 cells" is 4.05 points per cell. 2268/4 = 567 exactly; 560*4 = 2240. The companion counts behave differently again: NR 896/224 = 4.000, R 980/238 = 4.118. I cannot rebuild the denominator of the headline 93%.
- The two distortion parts do not multiply back to the total at the 1% the Figure 5 caption claims: on the Results' own quoted medians the product overshoots by 7.3% and 3.3% (R at N_ch 10 and 1e4) and 3.0% and 0.7% (IR). Diagnostics itself says only log det composes, so I cannot use the composition as a check.
- The least-squares crossing table and the "does noise cure it" medians disagree about the same boundary: at N_ch = 10 the k_off distortion is quoted as 1.14 at label 100, already below the 1.15 criterion, yet the crossing is placed at label 130; at N_ch = 1e4 it is 1.15 at label 1e5 and the crossing is placed at 1.59e5.
- IR's grid is "eleven noise levels" in Results and "twelve instrumental noise levels" in the Discussion.

I then carried on past each blocker on a guess, which is how the later ones (the mask, the bootstrap unit, the marginal-versus-C_ii ellipse) surfaced.
